EmuCoreR is a PlayStation emulator and game library powered by the SwanStation core, with quick setup, clean navigation, and a handheld-friendly interface.
Open the EmuCoreR GitHub repository for the app and project source.
Based on SwanStation, the libretro PlayStation emulator core.
Support ongoing development and future updates for EmuCoreR.
Open the author page on Google Play to see other apps from Sashkin Apps.
Open the official EmuCoreR website for news, guides and the latest project updates.
Enable vibration in supported games and on supported devices.
Runs a short vibration pulse using the current strength slider value.
Vibrate the handheld or phone body when the controller does not expose its own motor.
Play a short haptic tick when pressing on-screen controls.
Play a short vibration tick when pressing physical gamepad buttons.
Use Back button to exit game
Start the exit action instead of opening the game menu when you press Back.
Off by default. When enabled, the Android Back button uses the same exit action as Exit in the game menu, including the current confirmation behavior.
Ask before quick save or quick load.
Show draggable quick save and quick load buttons during gameplay

Adds two small draggable buttons on the emulation screen: one for quick save and one for quick load. Drag them anywhere to move them, and their positions are remembered. They work in every control mode, including when the touch controls are hidden or a physical gamepad is connected.
Let the emulation screen rotate between portrait and landscape instead of forcing landscape
When disabled, the emulation screen always stays in landscape. Enable it to play in portrait as well; the screen then follows device rotation. A global orientation lock overrides this option.
Locks the app orientation everywhere, including menus and the emulation screen. Auto follows the system rotation settings. Portrait and Landscape keep the whole app in the selected orientation.
Display the frame rate while playing.
Display the recently played games section on the home screen.
Display the search bar on the home screen.
Use English names from the EmuCoreR game database when they are available.
Long-press a setting name to restore that option to its default value.

Choose how a single physical controller should interact with touch controls. Replace touch makes one gamepad take Player 1 immediately, while Touch + Gamepad keeps touch on Player 1 and moves the single gamepad to Player 2. If two physical controllers are connected at the same time, they always become Player 1 and Player 2.
Prevents Android from dimming or locking the screen during play. Useful for long sessions and games with cutscenes, but it will use a little more battery if you leave the app open.

Lets supported games trigger controller rumble. It adds useful feedback in racing, combat, and impact-heavy games, but it can drain battery faster and some wireless pads may vibrate weakly or with slight delay.
Scales game rumble before it is sent to Android. Lower it for noisy handheld motors, or raise it when a controller feels too weak.
Sends a direct Android vibration request to the connected controller first, then to the phone or handheld fallback when enabled.

Some handheld controls report as a gamepad but expose vibration only through the device vibrator. This fallback keeps rumble working on those devices, but external controllers without rumble will vibrate the phone or handheld instead.
Adds light Android haptic feedback when an on-screen button, D-pad direction, or analog stick is first pressed. This affects control feel only and does not change in-game rumble.
Adds a short low-strength pulse on physical gamepad button presses. This is separate from game rumble, so supported games can still control normal controller vibration.
Shows a confirmation dialog before overwriting a save state or loading one. Turn it off for one-tap quick save and quick load.
Shows a quick-access row for the games you played last. Good if you bounce between a few titles often; turn it off if you want a cleaner home screen.
Shows the library search bar directly on the home screen. Leave it on for big libraries; turn it off if you prefer a cleaner layout and rarely search by name.

Uses English titles from EmuCoreR\'s GameIndex database for games that ship with Japanese or other regional names. This mainly helps imported releases read more clearly in the library, while games without an English database title keep their normal name.
Points EmuCoreR to a clean BIOS dump from your own PlayStation. The image must be exactly 512 KiB and use the .bin or .rom extension.

Adds folders to the game library. EmuCoreR scans every selected folder recursively and merges the results without duplicate file paths. Tap a listed folder to remove it. The current core supports .cue and .bin disc images.

Chooses the default cover type used when downloading artwork. Flat covers match the classic front-box look, while 3D Box uses angled box renders when the source provides them. 3D covers can look more dramatic, but availability may be slightly worse than flat art.

Overrides the built-in cover source used for automatic downloads. The URL should point directly to a folder that contains JPG covers named by game serial, for example SLUS-20312.jpg. Change this only if you host your own mirror or want to use a different compatible cover library.

Selects the graphics backend used for hardware rendering. Vulkan is usually the fastest on modern devices, OpenGL can be safer for compatibility on some GPUs, and Software is mainly a fallback for testing or games that break badly in hardware mode.

Controls how the final image is framed on your display. Auto follows the game, 4:3 keeps the original look for most PS1 titles, 16:9 suits widescreen-patched games, and Stretch should only be used if you do not mind geometric distortion.
Changes the size of on-screen buttons and sticks. Increase it if touch accuracy matters more than screen space; lower it if the overlay covers too much of the image.
Controls how solid or transparent the touch controls look. Lower opacity keeps the game view cleaner, while higher opacity makes buttons easier to see in dark or busy scenes.

Makes touch action buttons and shoulder buttons toggle their pressed state with a tap. This is useful for racing games where acceleration needs to stay held, while Start, Select, sticks, and the D-pad keep normal behavior.
Adjusts how quickly the left touch stick reaches stronger movement input. Higher values react faster, while lower values make small movement corrections easier.
Adjusts how quickly the right touch stick reaches stronger input. Higher values make camera or aim changes react faster, while lower values give you finer control.
Inverts the vertical axis for the left analog stick.
Inverts the vertical axis for the right analog stick.
Inverts the horizontal axis for the left analog stick.
Inverts the horizontal axis for the right analog stick.
Ignores small physical stick movements near the center. Raise it if your controller drifts on its own; keep it lower if you want faster response around center.
Adjusts how strongly the physical left stick responds after deadzone processing. Higher values reach full movement faster, while lower values make fine movement easier.
Adjusts how strongly the physical right stick responds after deadzone processing. Higher values make camera or aim movement react faster, while lower values give you finer control.
Maps the R2 analog trigger to upward movement on the right stick for both gamepads and on-screen controls. This can help racing games where throttle is bound to right stick up.
Maps the L2 analog trigger to downward movement on the right stick for both gamepads and on-screen controls. This can help racing games where brake is bound to right stick down.
Hides the touch overlay whenever a physical controller is active. This makes the screen cleaner, but turn it off if you still want touch buttons available while a controller is connected.
Uses a tighter overlay layout that takes less space around the edges of the screen. Good for smaller phones, but some players may prefer the larger spacing of the standard layout.
Changes the size of the analog stick touch areas. Larger values make them easier to grab during action-heavy games, while smaller values leave more room for the picture and nearby buttons.

Loads enabled cheat patches for the current game. Useful for widescreen, fan fixes, translations, or gameplay cheats, but the wrong patch version can break stability or apply to the wrong release of a game.
Shows a live performance overlay while the game is running. Use it when tuning settings or checking whether a slowdown comes from emulation speed, frame pacing, or the game itself.
Chooses between a simple FPS readout and a more detailed stats panel. Use the compact mode if you just want a quick speed check, or the extended mode when you are actively tuning performance.
Places the FPS or stats overlay in one of the four corners. Move it away from touch controls, HUD elements, subtitles, or minimaps so it stays readable without covering important game info.
Prevent the screen from dimming while playing.
Changes the text size of both the simple FPS counter and detailed statistics. Larger values also widen the detailed overlay to reduce wrapping.

Choose the individual values included in the detailed statistics overlay. App, build, and core versions are always shown first. CPU and GPU names with their load are read from the device when available.

Previews the selected press-and-release feel at the current strength.
Controls the device vibration strength used for touch control haptics. Raise it if the tick is too subtle, or lower it for quieter handheld play.

Reverses up and down aiming motion.

Aim converts phone rotation speed into the right analog stick for camera control in shooters and automatically returns to center when the phone stops moving. Steering converts the phone’s held tilt into the left analog stick for racing games and calibrates the current angle as center when gameplay starts. The selected mode is used only while a game is running and requires the corresponding motion sensor.
Controls how strongly phone movement deflects the emulated analog stick. Per-game overrides are recommended because games use different camera and steering response curves.
Filters sensor noise and hand shake. Lower values react faster; higher values feel steadier but add a small amount of latency.
This device does not expose the motion sensor required by the selected mode.

Sets the audio buffer used for playback. Lower values reduce sound delay, higher values are more stable on slower devices. Applied when the game starts.
Prefer the fastest AAudio output path

Requests the low-latency AAudio performance mode for the emulator audio stream. Reduces the delay between the console and the speaker, but uses more power and is less tolerant of background load. Applied when the game starts.

Soft is gentle, Balanced is the natural default, Crisp is short and precise, and Strong is deeper for weaker vibration motors.

Soft uses a gentle press and a very light release. Balanced gives a clear press with a lighter release and is the default. Crisp uses the shortest, sharpest pair for precise taps. Strong uses deeper, longer pulses for phones with weaker vibration motors. The strength slider scales the selected feel.

Smooths magnified textures on 3D objects. JINC2 and xBR are GPU shader upscalers and are heavier than bilinear filtering. Only affects the hardware renderers.
Scales the dithering pattern together with the internal resolution so gradients look smoother at higher resolution scales.
Forces 24-bit color output in the hardware renderers instead of the console\u2019s native 15-bit color. More accurate but slightly slower.
Forces progressive scan output. Fixes flicker on modern displays but can cause visual artifacts in games that rely on interlacing.
Runs PAL games using NTSC refresh timings. Can make some PAL releases run at the wrong speed.
Runs the software renderer in parallel for VRAM readbacks. Fixes corrupted textures and effects in some games at a small performance cost.
Selects the display aspect ratio used to present the game image.
Chooses how the visible area is cropped from the emulated framebuffer.
Shows core messages such as memory card writes, patches and compatibility warnings on screen.
Sets the emulated console region. Auto-Detect matches the region of the disc being played.
Recompiler (JIT) is the fastest and recommended. Interpreter modes are slower and intended for debugging.
Accelerates guest memory access. MMap is the fastest option on Android.
Emulates the CPU instruction cache in the recompiler. More accurate for self-modifying code, slightly slower.
Reads disc sectors ahead on a background thread, reducing loading hitches and frame spikes.
Rejects discs from a different region than the console. Disable to run imports and unlicensed discs.
Number of sectors prefetched ahead by the read thread. Higher values can improve loading but use more memory.
Uses the faster SPU audio hook. Disable only if you hear audio glitches or crackling.
Forwards game rumble to a connected controller or the device vibration motor.
Button combination used to toggle analog controller mode. Most games switch automatically.
Treats port 1 as a DualShock analog controller even for games that only use the digital controller.
L1 + R1 + L2 + R2 + Start + Select
Determines which region/hardware to emulate. Auto-Detect will use the region of the disc inserted.
Select which standard BIOS to use for NTSC-J.
Select which standard BIOS to use for NTSC-U.
Select which standard BIOS to use for PAL.
Skips the BIOS shell/intro, booting directly into the game. Usually safe to enable, but some games break.
Prevents discs from incorrect regions being read by the emulator. Usually safe to disable.
Reads CD-ROM sectors ahead asynchronously, reducing the risk of frame time spikes.
Automatically applies patches to disc images when they are present in the same directory. Currently only PPF patches are supported with this option. Requires the core to be restarted to apply.

Loads the disc image to RAM before starting emulation. May reduce hitching if you are running off a network share, at a cost of a greater startup time. As libretro provides no way to draw overlays, the emulator will appear to lock up while the image is preloaded.

Pre-caches CHD CD-ROM images to RAM without decompressing them. Unlike the preload option, this option supports M3U files. It is also faster and requires less RAM compared to preloading as it doesn\'t decompress the CHD.
Forcibly mutes both CD-DA and XA audio from the CD-ROM. Can be used to disable background music in some games.
Speeds up CD-ROM reads by the specified factor. Only applies to double-speed reads, and is ignored when audio is playing. May improve loading speeds in some games, at the cost of breaking others.
Speeds up CD-ROM seeks by the specified factor. May improve loading speeds in some games, at the cost of breaking others.
Which mode to use for CPU emulation. Recompiler provides the best performance.
Which renderer to use to emulate the GPU.
Scales internal VRAM resolution by the specified multiplier for the hardware renderer. Larger values are slower. Some games require 1x VRAM resolution or they will have rendering issues.
Uses a second thread for drawing graphics. Currently only available for the software renderer.

Runs the software renderer in parallel for VRAM readbacks. Some games may require this to be enabled to produce proper framebuffer effects (e.g. motion blur, battle swirls, etc.), or otherwise fix corrupted textures when using the hardware renderers. Requires the core to be restarted to apply.

Uses multisample antialiasing for rendering 3D objects. Can smooth out jagged edges on polygons at a lower cost to performance compared to increasing the resolution scale, but may be more likely to cause rendering errors in some games.
Disables dithering and uses the full 8 bits per channel of color information. May break rendering in some games.
Scales the dithering pattern with the internal rendering resolution, making it less noticeable. Usually safe to enable.
Disables interlaced rendering and display in the GPU. Some games can render in 480p this way, but others will break.
Forces PAL games to run at NTSC timings, i.e. 60hz. Some PAL games will run at their "normal" speeds, while others will break.
Switches back to 4:3 display aspect ratio when displaying 24-bit content, usually FMVs.
Smooths out blockiness between colour transitions in 24-bit content, usually FMVs. Only applies to the hardware renderers.
Smooths out the blockiness of magnified textures on 3D object by using bilinear filtering. Will have a greater effect on higher resolution scales. Only applies to the hardware renderers.
Increases the field of view from 4:3 to the chosen display aspect ratio in 3D games. For 2D games, or games which use pre-rendered backgrounds, this enhancement will not work as expected.
Reduces "wobbly" polygons by attempting to preserve the fractional component through memory transfers. Only works with the hardware renderers, and may not be compatible with all games.
Increases the precision of polygon culling, reducing the number of holes in geometry. Requires geometry correction enabled.
Uses perspective-correct interpolation for texture coordinates, straightening out warped textures. Requires geometry correction enabled.
Uses perspective-correct interpolation for vertex colors, which can improve visuals in some games, but cause rendering errors in others. Requires geometry correction enabled.
Attempts to reduce polygon Z-fighting by testing pixels against the depth values from PGXP. Low compatibility, but can work well in some games. Requires geometry correction enabled.
Uses screen coordinates as a fallback when tracking vertices through memory fails. May improve PGXP compatibility.
Tries to track vertex manipulation through the CPU. Some games require this option for PGXP to be effective. Very slow, and incompatible with the recompiler.
Enables additional precision for PGXP. May improve visuals in some games but break others.
Ignores precise positions if the difference exceeds this threshold.
Sets the threshold for the PGXP Depth Buffer.

Sets the preferred aspect ratio. Will only work when the \'Core Provided\' aspect ratio is selected inside RetroArch\'s Video settings. Will be forced to \'Corrected (NTSC)\' when using a Namco GunCon controller.
Sets the numerator for the custom aspect ratio, e.g. 4 in 4:3.
Sets the denominator for the custom aspect ratio, e.g. 3 in 4:3.
Changes how much of the image is cropped. Some games display garbage in the overscan area which is typically hidden.

Downsamples the rendered image prior to displaying it. Can improve overall image quality in mixed 2D/3D games, but should be disabled for pure 3D games. Only applies to the hardware renderers. The downsampling scale follows the Image Quality setting and only applies when it is above Native.

Controls when the hardware renderer\'s batch fragment shaders are compiled. \'Lazy\' (default) compiles them on a background thread while gameplay starts immediately; the previous frontend-blocking behaviour is preserved as \'Enabled\'. \'Disabled\' skips precompilation entirely and compiles each shader on the main thread the first time the game actually dispatches a draw using it - lowest startup latency, but brief stutters can occur during early gameplay when new shader permutations are encountered. Changing the texture filter recompiles the matrix and pays this cost again.
Enabled (block until done, like old behaviour)

Determines how far the CD-ROM thread will read ahead. Can reduce hitches on slow storage media or with compressed games.
Runs the emulated CPU faster or slower than native speed, which can improve framerates in some games. Will break other games and increase system requirements, use with caution.
Automatically disables enhancements on games which are incompatible.
Sets the level of information logged by the core.
Determines whether the CPU\'s instruction cache is simulated in the recompiler. Improves accuracy at a small cost to performance. If games are running too fast, try enabling this option.
Enables the generated code to directly jump between blocks without going through the dispatcher. Provides a measurable speed boost.
Uses page faults to determine hardware memory accesses at runtime. Can provide a significant performance improvement in some games, but make the core more difficult to debug.
CPU Recompiler Fast Memory Access Rewrite
Enables rewrites when CPU Recompiler Fast Memory Access is enabled. Can provide a measurable speed boost, but may cause the core to segfault on certain platforms.

Replace \'VRAM write textures\' with SwanStation-formatted texture packs from the \'swanstation/textures\' folder inside the frontend\'s system directory. This only works with the Vulkan and D3D11 (where available) renderers.
Preload VRAM write replacement textures to RAM

Simulates the system ahead of time and rolls back/replays to reduce input lag. Has very high system requirements. Most libretro frontends (including RetroArch) provide their own run-ahead implementation in their settings; the frontend version is generally more efficient and supports both single- and second-instance modes, so prefer it when available and leave this option at 0. Only enable this internal version if the frontend does not offer its own run-ahead, or to test against it.

Enables an additional 6MB of RAM, usually present on dev consoles. Games have to use a larger heap size for this additional RAM to be usable, and may break games which rely on memory mirroring, so it should only be used with compatible mods.

Use old routines for MDEC content. The newer routines may look better with some games, worse with others. As VRAM write texture replacements require either the old or new routines to function, it is advisable to toggle this setting to the routines required.

Drains all SPU samples to the frontend once per emulated frame, instead of pushing each chunk as the SPU produces it. This is faster and produces more even audio batching, and is the right choice for almost every game. A small number of titles (notably Formula 1 / Formula 1 \'97) hang at boot if audio is not delivered to the frontend mid-frame; the core auto-disables this option for those known titles, but if a game freezes at startup with audio enabled, try disabling this manually.
Caps emulation to the console\'s refresh rate. Turn off to run as fast as the device allows.
Overrides the emulated refresh rate. Auto follows the console region.
Overrides the emulated vertical refresh rate for this region. Adjust it slightly if NTSC audio crackles or PAL video stutters; the default follows the console standard.
Skips presenting rendered frames to reduce host load. Higher values are choppier but faster.
Trims pixels from the edges of the picture before scaling. Increase a value until the unwanted border disappears.
Enable widescreen patches for supported games

Loads widescreen patches when the current game has one available. This is usually better than stretching the image because it changes the game\'s camera and HUD logic instead of just distorting the final picture.
Enable no-interlacing patches for supported games
Applies no-interlacing patches where available. This is worth trying in games with combing, shimmer, or flicker from original interlaced output, but availability depends on the title.
